The US has removed its B-1 bombers from a British air base one week after five men were arrested nearby on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, a suspected plot that UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham claimed was likely backed by Iran.
The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers 90 miles (145 km) west of London, which had recently been used for US strikes on Iran. A Pentagon official said on Sunday they had now returned to their home bases in the US.
Five men arrested by British police over the incident, which remains shrouded in mystery, have been released on bail. A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, has also been released on bail.
Iran has said accusations it was involved in any plot are baseless, and its foreign minister, Abbas Aragchi, wrote on X: “I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You're barking up the wrong tree.”

Ethiopia’s history has come back to haunt it.
Late last month, seven armed groups - among them the Fano militia in Amhara, the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Oromo Liberation Army - announced the formation of the Ethiopian Peoples’ Forces Alliance for Survival, and vowed to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed.
Within days, Tigrayan forces had seized the airports in Mekelle, Axum and Shire, and opened fronts in Afar and Amhara. By 25 September, phone and internet lines in Tigray were cut. This time it was the TPLF, not Addis Ababa, that ordered the blackout.
Most commentary reads the new conflict as the collapse of the Pretoria agreement, a 2022 peace deal to end two years of war. But the story is much older than the Pretoria process and Abiy himself.
For nearly two centuries, Ethiopian politics has swung between a centre that wants to command, and regions that insist on ruling themselves. Each time the pendulum has pushed hard towards the centre, the peripheries have found a way to unite against it.

Among the many apps available on the Play Store, one stands out thanks to its heart‑shaped icon featuring a Palestinian flag: “Gaza Friendly”.
Created in June 2025, the label certifies shopkeepers involved in the boycott of products originating from the occupied Palestinian territories and marketed by companies supporting Israel’s settlement expansion.
To date, the app and its associated website list 80 businesses in France, mainly butchers, restaurants, bakeries, caterers, tea rooms and food distributors.
The list is updated regularly, and the app features an interactive map allowing consumers to locate certified shops near their homes.
The app, which has been downloaded more than 500 times so far, was created by Pierre-Amael Noailly Charny, a paediatrician of Tunisian origin from Lyon, in east-central France, along with a small group of friends.
Noailly Charny explains that shopkeepers who join Gaza Friendly can express their commitment to the Palestinian cause in a concrete way.

Iran's foreign ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, has said that the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz is the "main focus" of truce talks with Washington.
Speaking at a news conference, Baghaei said that Tehran is "focusing on the strait foremost", and that its primary concern is "to reach a solution and to have peace and stability restored within this waterway". He added that, by contrast, Washington's strategy to end the conflict is focused on Iran's nuclear file.
He told reporters that the return of International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors has not been discussed by Iran's leadership.
He noted that the peace process has been thwarted by the "volatility and fluctuation" of Washington's decision-making.
“This is reflected in their conflicting statements as well as their fluctuating demands. This is a problem faced not only by Iran, but by all the countries dealing with the United States. These countries are openly complaining about the crisis,” said Baghaei said.
Meanwhile, Tasnim news agency reports that Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said at a meeting with foreign ambassadors that there is "no military solution or any solution based on new sanctions" to the seven-month-long conflict.
“If our enemies again choose the path of military confrontation, our response will be stronger than before, and we will defend ourselves with even more force,” Araghchi said.
He added that Tehran is “serious about finding diplomatic solutions, just as we are serious about defending ourselves”.

For more than three years, Sudan has been trapped in a war that has shattered cities, emptied villages and pushed millions into displacement. Since fighting erupted between the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in 2023, international diplomacy produced no shortage of conferences, ceasefire proposals and mediation initiatives.
Yet each new round of negotiations has been overtaken by renewed violence on the ground. The human cost has continued to rise, with more than 150,000 people estimated dead, over 14 million displaced, and famine spreading across parts of Sudan.
Against this backdrop, the EU has increasingly turned to sanctions as its principal instrument of engagement. Its latest package, adopted in July 2026, represents a notable shift. Rather than expanding the practice of blacklisting individuals and companies, Brussels moved to target Sudan's war economy, banning imports of Sudanese gold and prohibiting exports of mercury and cyanide used in gold extraction.

Gaza aid delay causes chronic shortage of medical supplies, WHO says
Getting humanitarian aid through Israel into Gaza is layered with "delay after delay", the World Health Organisation said Friday, as it decried "chronic shortages" of medical supplies.
Reinhilde Van de Weerdt, the WHO's representative in the Palestinian territories, said the health situation in the Gaza Strip "remains utterly dire", with none of its hospitals fully functional.
"Not enough humanitarian aid is entering Gaza, and definitely not enough to allow for a meaningful expansion and restoration of health services," she told reporters in Geneva, speaking from Jerusalem.
She said Israel's approval system for medical and other humanitarian supplies was proving a major bottleneck.
"It is laborious, time-consuming, with no guaranteed results," she said.
Based on the WHO's latest analysis, large volumes of medical supplies wait for clearance for a median of 74 days, said Van de Weerdt, adding that if it is not, "than we start that lengthy, cumbersome process all over again".
She added that the approval system kept changing, with new regulations introduced.
Van de Weerdt said standard health kits used worldwide had the lowest approval rate, while X-ray machines, sterilisation equipment and spare parts for CT scans and other essential machinery "get rejected regularly".
"In just the last six months alone, one shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices was rejected four separate times," she said.
However, medicines move "relatively well", with almost 87 percent approved and one percent rejected, she added.
"It's not one single blockage. It's a system, layered with delay after delay... and on the other side of every one of these delays is a patient who is waiting," she said.
"We need the unimpeded and predicable entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza, at scale.
Report by AFP

US sanctions three persons, two charities over alleged Hamas funding
The United States has issued sanctions against three individuals and two France-based charities that it said were part of a network that raised more than $2 million for Hamas, and announced six arrests.
"These designations expose a sophisticated, multi‑year financing architecture that moved more than $2 million to Hamas through deceptive charitable fronts and cryptocurrency channels, demonstrating the organisation's persistent ability to adapt its fundraising mechanisms to evade detection," the US Treasury said in a statement.
Those sanctioned include Saleem Abdallah Saleem al-Zaq, identified as a Hamas member who oversees the financial network and works with the group's media office.
The US Justice Department said French authorities had also arrested sanctioned individuals Faouzi Barika and Amel Oualid, who are linked to the France-based charities Association Baraka and Ensemble C Mieux.
Both charities were also sanctioned in Friday's action. A third person, Nordine Barika, was also arrested by French authorities in the case, the DOJ said.
"Faouzi Barika and Amel Oualid operate from France, where they run purported charities ostensibly to raise money for humanitarian purposes to aid Gazan civilians," the US Treasury said.
In the United States, authorities arrested three men for their alleged funding of Hamas through the network, the DOJ said.
US authorities said the network had raised more than $2 million from 2020 to 2026, of which $1.5 million was raised after the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas on Israel.
Report by AFP

Iraq given US exemption for Iranian flights to and from holy city
The United States has granted sanctions exemptions for some Iranian airlines to operate flights to Iraq's holy city of Najaf, the Iraqi prime minister's office said on Friday.
It said Baghdad had secured "an agreement allowing Iranian airlines, with the exception of Mahan Air, to operate 40 flights daily to and from Najaf" , a city sacred to Shia Muslims.
The US announced sweeping new sanctions targeting Iranian airlines last month as part of its efforts to pressure Iran's economy, with the two sides still to make peace in Washington's war on Tehran.
Last week, Najaf airport suspended all Iranian flights in cooperation with the sanctions, leaving travellers scrambling for alternative routes.
